lines.text: That's an offshore wind turbine. Over 200 meters tall, and miles from shore.
So how do engineers build something this massive, in the middle of the sea?
It starts underwater. A steel tube called a monopile gets driven deep into the seabed.
Then a transition piece slides on top, and the first tower section bolts to it.
Next comes a special ship. It parks, then lowers its steel legs to the seabed.
Then it lifts its whole hull above the waves. Now the crane stands on solid ground, not a rocking boat.
The crane picks up the tower sections one at a time, and each flange gets aligned and bolted down.
Then the nacelle, the engine room of the turbine, goes up on top.
Blades are the delicate part. Each one is lifted alone, toward the hub, slowly.
A strong gust can stop the whole job. So crews wait for a calm weather window.
Once all three blades are on, the turbine is built. Then come the cables.
Power runs along the seabed to a substation, and from there to shore.
A ship that stands on the seabed. That is how you build in the sea. Subscribe for more.
